name: 6-OXO (4-androstene-3,6,17-trione)

lead: 6-OXO is an oral supplement ingredient described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor. Steroid and prohormone users take it to limit estrogen rise and gynecomastia risk and to speed recovery after cycles, aiming at a higher testosterone-to-estrogen ratio and a leaner muscular look.

It is reported to permanently inactivate aromatase, lowering estradiol and raising LH and testosterone. The main human study, a 2007 eight-week trial in resistance-trained men, was uncontrolled and partly industry-funded; it found large rises in free testosterone and DHT but no change in body composition.

paras: It is taken as an oral supplement, typically during or after steroid or prohormone cycles. Users describe it as part of a recovery or estrogen-control routine.
The FDA stated products containing it are adulterated, and Health Canada warned in 2008 of a blood-clotting risk. Acne is a listed possible effect. It is banned by WADA.

chain: Less gyno risk, leaner muscle look
angle.text: 6-OXO is used by steroid and prohormone users who say it limits estrogen rise, supports recovery and keeps the muscle look leaner. A 2007 uncontrolled study showed hormone shifts without body-composition change.

lead: 6-OXO (4-androstene-3,6,17-trione, also 4-AT) is an oral supplement ingredient sold to bodybuilders as an aromatase inhibitor, a compound that blocks the enzyme that converts testosterone into estrogen. People use it to look better in two ways: by keeping estrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia (breast tissue growth) and water retention in check during steroid or prohormone use, and by raising the testosterone-to-estrogen ratio in the hope of building more muscle.[1]

Wikipedia describes it as a potent, irreversible aromatase inhibitor, and says users also take it after a cycle to shorten recovery of testicular function.[1] The main human study, a 2007 eight-week trial in resistance-trained men from Baylor University, reported large increases in free testosterone and DHT and a higher testosterone-to-estradiol ratio, with no change in body composition or safety markers. It had no control group and was partly funded by commercial 4-AT producers.[1]

Regulators have acted on it. The World Anti-Doping Agency lists it as banned, a 2006 FDA warning letter argued that marketing it violated federal law, and in 2008 Health Canada told consumers to stop using 6-OXO after a reported case of seizures and brain blood clots.[1][2]
infobox: FDA warning letter 2006; Health Canada warning 2008; WADA-banned [1][2]

paras: Users, often of steroids or prohormones, report taking it to offset estrogen increases during a cycle, which they say reduces gynecomastia risk and water retention, and afterwards to shorten recovery from testicular suppression.[1] Because testosterone is myotropic and estradiol is not, proponents argue a higher ratio could favour muscle, although Wikipedia notes no human or animal studies have tested an anabolic effect of 4-AT.[1]
4-AT is described as permanently binding and inactivating aromatase in fat and other peripheral tissue. Lower estradiol is reported to raise luteinizing hormone, which in turn raises testosterone.[1]

Analytical papers in 2005 described detection of 4-AT and its metabolites in urine, and WADA bans it.[1] A July 2006 FDA warning letter argued that marketing it violated federal law, making products adulterated.[1]

In June 2008 Health Canada warned consumers not to use 6-OXO, citing risks including seizures and blood clots in the brain that can cause lasting disability, based on one Canadian case. The product is not authorized for sale in Canada, and the agency said it was acting to stop further imports.[2] Acne is listed as a possible side effect.[1]

A related FDA action in March 2004 declared androstenedione supplements adulterated and led to warning letters to 23 companies, which forms part of the regulatory background for prohormone-type supplements.[3]

A 2007 eight-week study of resistance-trained men gave two dose levels of 6-OXO and reported rises of roughly 84 to 90 percent in free testosterone, significant rises in DHT and the free testosterone-to-estradiol ratio, only partial aromatase inhibition, and no effect on body composition or clinical safety markers. Elevated DHT fell after a three-week washout. There was no control group and two commercial 4-AT producers partly funded the work.[1]
